biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a bequest as “Something left by will; a legacy.” Scripture honours the man who provides beyond his own life: “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children” (Pro 13:22). A bequest takes effect only at death, as the apostle says of every will: “For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator” (Heb 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BEQUEST, something left by will; a legacy.
webster_full: BEQUEST', noun Something left by will; a legacy.
scriptures: A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
Heb 9:16
For where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator.
Heb 9:17
For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth.
corruption_summary: A bequest is a dead man’s word still speaking; Scripture expects a good man to leave one.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster gives the word one sense: “Something left by will.” The gift is fixed before death and delivered after it.
The Lord’s own testament is in force because the Testator died (Heb 9:16-17). A father who leaves his children’s children an inheritance follows the pattern of Pro 13:22.
roots_summary: Something left by will; a legacy.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): something left by will; a legacy.
A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children (Pro 13:22).

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a codicil as “A writing by way of supplement to a will.” Scripture never names a codicil. It does set down the rule for a confirmed covenant between men: “Though it be but a man’s covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto” (Gal 3:15). God’s word admits no supplement from man: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you” (Deu 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CODICIL, a writing by way of supplement to a will.
webster_full: CODICIL, noun A writing by way of supplement to a will.
scriptures: Gal 3:15
Brethren, I speak after the manner of men; Though it be but a man's covenant, yet if it be confirmed, no man disannulleth, or addeth thereto.
Heb 9:17
For a testament is of force after men are dead: otherwise it is of no strength at all while the testator liveth.
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
corruption_summary: A man may add a codicil to his own will; no man may add one to God’s.
corruption_paragraphs: A codicil is the testator’s own act. Only the man who made the will may supplement it, and only while he lives (Heb 9:17).
The Lord’s covenant is confirmed, and no man “addeth thereto” (Gal 3:15). Moses forbade adding to the word (Deu 4:2).
roots_summary: A writing that supplements a will.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a writing by way of supplement to a will.
No man disannulleth, or addeth thereto (Gal 3:15).
usage: A writing by way of supplement to a will

pos: n. & adj. (word of mouth; a prisoner’s promise)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines parole as “Properly, a word; hence, in a legal sense, words or oral declaration; word of mouth.” As an adjective it means “Given by word of mouth; oral; not written.” In military affairs it is “a promise given by a prisoner of war, when he has leave to depart from custody, that he will return at the time appointed, unless discharged.” A parole stands on a man’s bare word, and Scripture binds a man to it: “he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth” (Num 30:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PAROLE, a word; word of mouth; oral declaration; in military affairs, a prisoner’s promise to return at the time appointed.
webster_full: PAROLE, noun [Latin parabola.]
1. Properly, a word; hence, in a legal sense, words or oral declaration; word of mouth. Formerly, conveyances were made by parol or word of mouth only.
2. Pleadings in a suit; as anciently all pleadings were viva voce or ore tenus.
The parole may demur.
PARO'LE, adjective Given by word of mouth; oral; not written; as Parole evidence.
[It would be well to write this word Parole, in uniformity with the following, there being no good reason for a distinction.]

PARO'LE, noun [See Parol ] Word of mouth. In military affairs, a promise given by a prisoner of war, when he has leave to depart from custody, that he will return at the time appointed, unless discharged. A parole is properly a verbal or unwritten promise, but I believe it is customary to take a promise in writing.
scriptures: Num 30:2
If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
corruption_summary: A parole is only as good as the man who gives it; Scripture asks that his word need no writing.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster notes that a parole is “properly a verbal or unwritten promise.” The released prisoner is trusted on his word alone.
Christ asks that a man’s plain yea and nay be enough (Mat 5:37). The man God receives “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4).
roots_summary: Latin parabola: a word; then a promise given by word of mouth.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): properly, a word.
Webster: a promise given by a prisoner of war.
He shall not break his word (Num 30:2).

pos: n. (a writ calling up a cause to a superior court)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines certiorari as “A writ issuing out of Chancery, Kings Bench or other superior court, to call up the records of an inferior court, or remove a cause there depending, that it may be tried in the superior court.” It is granted “upon complaint of a party, that he has not received justice, or that he cannot have an impartial trial, in the inferior court.” Scripture names no such writ, but it orders courts in ranks: “every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge” (Exo 18:22). Paul, refusing a biased hearing, said, “I appeal unto Caesar” (Act 25:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CERTIORARI, a writ from a superior court calling up the records of an inferior court, granted when a party has not received justice there.
webster_full: CERTIORARI, noun A writ issuing out of Chancery, Kings Bench or other superior court, to call up the records of an inferior court, or remove a cause there depending, that it may be tried in the superior court. This writ is obtained upon complaint of a party, that he has not received justice, or that he cannot have an impartial trial, in the inferior court.
scriptures: And let them judge the people at all seasons: and it shall be, that every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge: so shall it be easier for thyself, and they shall bear the burden with thee.
Deu 17:8

If there arise a matter too hard for thee in judgment, between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke, being matters of controversy within thy gates: then shalt thou arise, and get thee up into the place which the LORD thy God shall choose;

For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar.
corruption_summary: Certiorari exists because lower courts can fail; Scripture provided a higher bench for the hard case.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster ties the writ to a party who “cannot have an impartial trial” below. The remedy is a higher court, not private vengeance.
Moses sent the matter “too hard for thee in judgment” up to the judge at the place the LORD would choose (Deu 17:8). Paul used Rome’s own higher court (Act 25:11).
roots_summary: A writ to call up a cause to a higher court.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): to call up the records of an inferior court.
Every great matter they shall bring unto thee (Exo 18:22).

pos: n. (a bar raised by one’s own act)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines estoppel as “In law, a stop; a plea in bar, grounded on a man’s own act or deed, which estops or precludes him from averring any thing to the contrary.” Christ judges on the same principle: “Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant” (Luk 19:22). “For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned” (Mat 12:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ESTOPPEL, a stop; a plea in bar grounded on a man’s own act or deed, which precludes him from averring the contrary.
webster_full: ESTOP'PEL, noun In law, a stop; a plea in bar, grounded on a man's own act or deed, which estops or precludes him from averring any thing to the contrary.
If a tenant for years levies a fine to another person, it shall work as an estoppel to the cognizor.
scriptures: And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:
For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.
And David said unto him, Thy blood be upon thy head; for thy mouth hath testified against thee, saying, I have slain the LORD'S anointed.
corruption_summary: Estoppel holds a man to what he has said and done; at the judgment no man can unsay his own words.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s estoppel rests on “a man’s own act or deed.” The law will not let him plead against his own deed.
David condemned the Amalekite on his own report: “thy mouth hath testified against thee” (2Sa 1:16). The servant who hid his pound was judged out of his own mouth (Luk 19:22).
roots_summary: A stop: a man barred by his own act or deed.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): in law, a stop; a plea in bar.
Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee (Luk 19:22).

pos: n. (owner of land with tenants; an innkeeper)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a landlord as “The lord of a manor or of land; the owner of land who has tenants under him.” A second sense is “The master of an inn or tavern.” Scripture reminds every owner that his title is held under God: “The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine” (Lev 25:23). The good Samaritan paid “the host” of the inn and promised to repay whatever more he spent (Luk 10:35).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): LANDLORD, the owner of land who has tenants under him; the master of an inn or tavern.
webster_full: LAND'LORD, noun
1. The lord of a manor or of land; the owner of land who has tenants under him.
2. The master of an inn or tavern.
scriptures: The land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.

Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:
Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;
And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.
corruption_summary: Every landlord is himself a tenant of God and owes his tenants justice.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s landlord “has tenants under him.” Scripture puts every owner under the Owner of the land (Lev 25:23).
Christ’s householder “let it out to husbandmen” and looked for fruit (Mat 21:33). The prophet pronounced woe on the man “that useth his neighbour’s service without wages” (Jer 22:13).
roots_summary: The lord of land; the owner with tenants under him.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the owner of land who has tenants under him.
Webster: the master of an inn or tavern.
For the land is mine (Lev 25:23).

pos: n. (one versed in the arts of government)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a statesman as “A man versed in the arts of government; usually, one eminent for political abilities; a politician.” He adds “One employed in public affairs.” Scripture names the qualities God requires in such men: “able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exo 18:21). Joseph and Daniel served pagan kings as statesmen; of Daniel it is written, “an excellent spirit was in him” (Dan 6:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): STATESMAN, a man versed in the arts of government; one eminent for political abilities; one employed in public affairs.
webster_full: STATESMAN, noun [state and man.]
1. A man versed in the arts of government; usually, one eminent for political abilities; a politician.
2. A small landholder.
3. One employed in public affairs.
scriptures: Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens:
Deu 1:13
Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you.
Dan 6:3
Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
corruption_summary: The statesman is measured by the fear of God and truth before skill; a skilled politician without them is a danger.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s first sense joins skill, “versed in the arts of government”, to public trust. Scripture asks first for character (Exo 18:21).
“When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2). Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes “because an excellent spirit was in him” (Dan 6:3).
roots_summary: State and man: a man versed in governing.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a man versed in the arts of government.
Webster: one employed in public affairs.
Able men, such as fear God (Exo 18:21).
usage: A man versed in the arts of government

pos: n. (a fortified town; a town with corporate privileges)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a borough as “Originally, a fortified city or town.” In later use it is given “to such towns and villages as send representatives or burgesses to Parliament.” In Connecticut it is “a town or a part of a town, or a village, incorporated with certain privileges, distinct from those of other towns and of cities.” Scripture records towns ruled in parts, as “Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem” (Neh 3:9), and tells God’s people to “seek the peace of the city” where they dwell (Jer 29:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BOROUGH, originally a fortified city or town; a town that sends burgesses to Parliament; in Connecticut, a town or village incorporated with certain privileges.
webster_full: BOROUGH, noun. bur'ro. [Latin parcus, saving.] Originally, a fortified city or town; hence a hill, for hills were selected for places of defense. But in later times, the term city was substituted to denote an episcopal town, in which was the see of a bishop, and that of borough was retained for the rest. At present, the name is given appropriately to such towns and villages as send representatives or burgesses to Parliament.

BOROUGH, noun bur'ro. In Saxon times, a main pledge, or association of men, who were sureties or free pledges to the king for the good behavior of each other, and if any offense was committed in their district, they were bound to have the offender forthcoming. The association of ten men was called a tithing, or decenary; the presiding man was called the tithing man, or head-borough; or in some places, borsholder, borough's elder. This society was called also friburg, free burg, frank pledge. Ten tithings formed a hundred, consisting of that number of sureties, and this denomination is still given to the districts, comprehended in the association. The term seems to have been used both for the society and for each surety. The word main, hand, which is attached to this society, or their mutual assurance, indicates that the agreement was ratified by shaking hands.

Some writers have suggested that the application of this word to towns sprung from these associations, and of course was posterior to them in time. But the word was used for a town or castle in other nations, and in Asia, doubtless long before the origin of the frank pledge.

In Connecticut, this word, borough is used for a town or a part of a town, or a village, incorporated with certain privileges, distinct from those of other towns and of cities; as the borough of Bridgeport.
In Scotland, a borough is a body corporate, consisting of the inhabitants of a certain district, erected by the Sovereign, with a certain jurisdiction.

Boroughs are erected to be held of the sovereign, as is generally the case of royal boroughs; or of the superior of the lands included, as in the case of boroughs of regality and barony. Royal boroughs are generally erected for the advantage of trade.
BOROUGH ENGLISH, is a customary descent of lands and tenements to the youngest son, instead of the eldest; or if the owner leaves no son, to the youngest brother.
Borough-head, the same as head-borough, the chief of a borough.
scriptures: Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Neh 3:9
And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem.
But Paul said, I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city: and, I beseech thee, suffer me to speak unto the people.
corruption_summary: A borough is a local body with its own privileges; the Christian seeks its peace and keeps its charter.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s Saxon borough was “a main pledge, or association of men, who were sureties or free pledges to the king for the good behavior of each other.” Neighbours answered for one another.
Paul did not despise his home town: “a citizen of no mean city” (Act 21:39). Nehemiah’s rulers each repaired their own part of the wall (Neh 3:9).
roots_summary: Latin parcus: a fortified town, then a chartered town.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): originally, a fortified city or town.
Seek the peace of the city (Jer 29:7).

pos: n. (Roman chief magistrate; a state’s agent abroad)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a consul first as “The chief magistrate of the Ancient Roman Republic, invested with regal authority for one year.” In modern usage it is “a person commissioned by a king or state to reside in a foreign country as an agent or representative, to protect the rights, commerce, merchants and seamen of the state.” Scripture never names a consul. It shows Roman magistrates over the provinces, as when “Gallio was the deputy of Achaia” (Act 18:12), and one of them, Sergius Paulus, “desired to hear the word of God” (Act 13:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CONSUL, the chief magistrate of the Roman Republic; a person commissioned to reside in a foreign country to protect the rights and commerce of his state.
webster_full: CONSUL, noun [Latin , to consult.]
1. The chief magistrate of the Ancient Roman Republic, invested with regal authority for one year. There were two consuls, annually chosen in the campus Martius.

2. In modern usage, the name consul is given to a person commissioned by a king or state to reside in a foreign country as an agent or representative, to protect the rights, commerce, merchants and seamen of the state, and to aid the government in any commercial transactions with such foreign country.
3. An adviser. [Not well authorized.]
scriptures: And when Gallio was the deputy of Achaia, the Jews made insurrection with one accord against Paul, and brought him to the judgment seat,
Act 13:7
Which was with the deputy of the country, Sergius Paulus, a prudent man; who called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God.
Then the deputy, when he saw what was done, believed, being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
corruption_summary: A consul serves his own nation in a foreign land; the Christian holds a like office as an ambassador for Christ (2Co 5:20).
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s modern consul resides abroad “to protect the rights, commerce, merchants and seamen of the state.” He lives among strangers for the sake of his own people.
Roman magistrates heard Paul’s case and some believed (Act 13:12). The magistrate “is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4).
roots_summary: Latin, to consult: the counselling magistrate, then a state’s agent abroad.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the chief magistrate of the Ancient Roman Republic.
Webster: a person commissioned by a king or state to reside in a foreign country.
Gallio was the deputy of Achaia (Act 18:12).

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines splendor as “Great brightness; brilliant luster; as the splendor of the sun.” It is also “Great show of richness and elegance; magnificence” and “Pomp; parade.” True splendor belongs to God: “thou art clothed with honour and majesty” (Psa 104:1). Christ set the splendor of kings beside the lilies: “even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these” (Mat 6:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SPLENDOR, great brightness; brilliant luster; great show of richness and elegance; magnificence; pomp; eminence.
webster_full: SPLENDOR, noun [Latin See Plant and Planet.]
1. Great brightness; brilliant luster; as the splendor of the sun.
2. Great show of richness and elegance; magnificence; as the splendor of equipage or of royal robes.
3. Pomp; parade; as the splendor of a procession or of ceremonies.
4. Brilliance; eminence; as the splendor of a victory.
scriptures: Bless the LORD, O my soul. O LORD my God, thou art very great; thou art clothed with honour and majesty.
Mat 6:29
And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them.
And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.
And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.
corruption_summary: Splendor that points to God is worship; splendor a man takes for himself is pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Herod sat “arrayed in royal apparel” and took the people’s praise (Act 12:21). He was struck “because he gave not God the glory” (Act 12:23).
The new Jerusalem needs no sun: “the glory of God did lighten it” (Rev 21:23).
roots_summary: Great brightness, then magnificence and pomp.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): great brightness; brilliant luster.
Webster: great show of richness and elegance; magnificence.
Thou art clothed with honour and majesty (Psa 104:1).

pos: v. & n. (to lay at rest; rest; quiet)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines repose as a verb, “To lay at rest”, and “To lay; to rest, as the mind, in confidence or trust.” As a noun it is “Sleep; rest; quiet” and “Rest of mind; tranquility; freedom from uneasiness.” Scripture grounds such rest in God alone: “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” (Psa 4:8). “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee” (Isa 26:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): REPOSE, v. to lay at rest; to rest the mind in confidence; n. sleep; rest; quiet; rest of mind; tranquility.
webster_full: REPO'SE, verb transitive s as z. [Latin repono, reposui.]
1. To lay at rest.
- After the toil of battle, to repose your wearied virtue.
2. To lay; to rest, as the mind, in confidence or trust; as, to repose trust or confidence in a person's veracity.
3. To lay up; to deposit; to lodge; as pebbles reposed in cliffs.
4. To place in confidence.
REPO'SE, verb intransitive
1. To lie at rest; to sleep.
Within a thicket I repos'd.
2. To rest in confidence. I repose on the faith and honor of a friend.
3. To lie; to rest; as trap reposing on sand.
REPO'SE, noun
1. A lying at rest.
2. Sleep; rest; quiet.
3. Rest of mind; tranquility; freedom from uneasiness.
4. Cause of rest.
5. In poetry, a rest; a pause.
6. In painting, harmony of colors, as when nothing glaring appears.
scriptures: Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Pro 3:24
When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.
corruption_summary: Repose is rest that trusts; Scripture puts its ground in God, not in circumstances.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster joins rest to trust: to repose is “to rest, as the mind, in confidence or trust.” A man reposes in what he believes will hold.
Christ offers it to the weary: “I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28).
roots_summary: Latin repono: to lay back, to lay at rest.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): to lay at rest.
Webster: rest of mind; tranquility; freedom from uneasiness.
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep (Psa 4:8).

pos: n. (a freeholder; a man free born)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a yeoman as “A common man, or one of the plebeians, of the first or most respectable class; a freeholder; a man free born.” He notes that “A yeoman in England is considered as next in order to the gentry.” The yeoman’s ideal is Israel’s under Solomon, when men “dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree” (1Ki 4:25). Paul claimed the same standing: “But I was free born” (Act 22:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): YEOMAN, a common man of the first or most respectable class; a freeholder; a man free born; an officer of middle rank; a ship’s storekeeping officer.
webster_full: YEOMAN, noun [See Common.]

1. A common man, or one of the plebeians, of the first or most respectable class; a freeholder; a man free born. A yeoman in England is considered as next in order to the gentry. The word is Little Used in the United States, unless as a title in law proceedings and instruments, designating occupation, and this only in particular states. But yeomanry is much used.
2. An officer in the kings household, of a middle rank between a gentleman and a groom.
3. In ships, an inferior officer under the boatswain, gunner or carpenters, charged with the stowage, account and distribution of the stores.
4. A name or title of certain soldiers; as yeomen of the guard.
scriptures: And Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
Mic 4:4
But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it.
And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
corruption_summary: The yeoman holds his own land and answers for it; Scripture makes that the picture of peace.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s yeoman is “a freeholder”, owning the ground he works. Micah’s promise is every man under his own vine, “and none shall make them afraid” (Mic 4:4).
The freeholder must tend what is his: “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23).
roots_summary: A common man of the first class; a freeholder.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a freeholder; a man free born.
Every man under his vine and under his fig tree (1Ki 4:25).
